o: We must support two operations: store a dictionary of distinct words, then answer queries: can we change **exactly one** character of the query word to obtain some stored word? Exactly one means a word equal to the query does NOT count (see `search("hello")` returning false), and lengths must match (so "hell" fails against "hello"). Constraints are tiny: at most 100 words of length ≤ 100, and 100 searches, so even an O(words × length) scan per query (~10^6 ops) is fine. This means we don't need anything fancy like a trie with clever pruning — grouping by length plus a direct comparison is optimal in practice.
k: A word matches iff it has the same length as the query and differs in exactly one position.
Grouping dictionary words by length lets each search only compare words of matching length.
Given tiny constraints (≤100 words, ≤100 chars), brute-force comparison per query is fast enough; tries add complexity without benefit here.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force with length buckets
a.i: For each search, compare the query against every dictionary word of the same length. Two words are a valid match if they differ in exactly one character position — count mismatches while scanning and check it equals 1. Bucketing words by length avoids wasted comparisons on words that can never match.
s: Store all words in a hash map from length to list of words.
On search(word), get the bucket for len(word); if absent return false.
For each candidate, count positions where characters differ.
Return true as soon as some candidate has exactly one mismatch.
If no candidate qualifies, return false.
a.t: O(N·L) per search where N is the number of same-length words and L is word length — each candidate needs one linear comparison; buildDict is O(total characters).
a.sp: O(total characters) to store the dictionary.

a.n: Approach 2: Generalized neighbor set (precompute all one-edit variants)
a.i: Precompute, for every dictionary word, all strings obtained by replacing exactly one character with any other letter ('a'–'z'), storing them in a hash set. A search succeeds iff the query's generated variant set intersects this set. This shifts work to build time and makes each search nearly O(L·26) hash lookups — great when searches vastly outnumber dictionary size.
s: During buildDict, for each word and each position i, replace w[i] with every letter except w[i]; insert the result into a set.
On search(word), generate all L×25 one-edit variants of the query.
Return true if any generated variant is in the set, else false.
a.t: buildDict is O(D·L²·26) due to string construction per variant (D words, length L); each search is O(L²·26) for generating and hashing variants.
a.sp: O(D·L²·26) worst case for the neighbor set, though duplicates collapse in practice.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1: it's simple, obviously correct, and within constraints it's effectively optimal. Mention Approach 2 as a trade-off discussion — it front-loads work into build time and gives near-constant-per-candidate searches, which matters if there were millions of queries or a huge dictionary. Common pitfalls: forgetting that an exact match (zero differences) must return false since we change *exactly* one character; comparing words of different lengths; and off-by-one issues when mutating a char array during variant generation (always restore the original character). Edge cases: single-character words (any different single-letter word matches), and duplicate-length groups. Likely follow-ups: handle up to k changes (generalize mismatch counting or BFS over edit distance), stream the dictionary, or use a trie with DFS pruning for very large dictionaries.
